items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than the pupils (B) poured out of the classroom, (C) leaving behind a pile of (D) unfinished worksheets on the teacher's desk.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
unfinished worksheets on the teacher's desk
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: After a negative adverbial such as No sooner at the start of a sentence, subject and auxiliary invert: No sooner had the bell rung than….

items.q: The coach (A) insisted that every player (B) arrives at the stadium an hour early (C) so as to warm up properly (D) before Saturday's final.
options: arrives at the stadium an hour early
so as to warm up properly
items.correction: arrive at the stadium an hour early
items.explanation: Verbs of demand such as insist, suggest, demand take the subjunctive (base form) in the that-clause: insisted that every player arrive.

items.q: (A) After climbing for six hours through deep snow, (B) the summit was finally reached by the team, (C) whose members had barely slept (D) the night before.
options: After climbing for six hours through deep snow
the summit was finally reached by the team
items.correction: the team finally reached the summit
items.explanation: The participle clause After climbing… must describe the subject of the main clause; the summit did not climb, so the team must be the subject (otherwise the modifier dangles).

items.q: If Minh (A) had accepted the scholarship (B) abroad three years ago, he (C) would have been living in Lyon now (D) instead of commuting to a job he dislikes.
options: would have been living in Lyon now
instead of commuting to a job he dislikes
items.correction: would be living in Lyon now
items.explanation: A mixed conditional: a past condition (had accepted) with a present result marked by now takes would + be, not would have been.

items.q: I wish I (A) had taken chemistry more seriously at school, (B) because now I can (C) barely follow the lectures, and if only the professor (D) will slow down.
items.explanation: After wish / if only, a complaint about someone's present behaviour uses would, never will: if only the professor would slow down.

items.q: The volunteers spent the summer (A) clearing footpaths, (B) repairing dry-stone walls (C) and to plant native hedges (D) along the reserve's boundary.
items.explanation: Items joined by and must be parallel: two -ing forms (clearing, repairing) require a third, planting, not an infinitive.

items.q: (A) What alarms the marine biologists most (B) are the speed (C) at which the coral has bleached (D) since their last survey in March.
options: What alarms the marine biologists most
at which the coral has bleached
since their last survey in March
items.explanation: A what-clause used as a subject is singular, so the verb of the cleft sentence must be is: What alarms them most is the speed….

items.q: Surprisingly, (A) fewer information has been published about the deep-sea vents (B) than about the surface of Mars, (C) even though they lie (D) only a few kilometres beneath us.
options: than about the surface of Mars
only a few kilometres beneath us
items.explanation: Information is uncountable, so it takes less, not fewer; fewer is reserved for plural countable nouns.

items.q: Before submitting (A) their final essays, (B) the students were asked (C) to make thorough research (D) into local dialects.
items.explanation: Research collocates with do or carry out, never make; make research is a classic collocation error.

items.q: (A) Only after the last guest had left (B) and the lights had been dimmed (C) the caretaker noticed that (D) the antique clock had gone missing.
options: Only after the last guest had left
and the lights had been dimmed
the antique clock had gone missing
items.explanation: When Only after… opens the sentence, the main clause inverts subject and auxiliary: did the caretaker notice.

items.q: Hardly (A) had the expedition set up camp (B) than a blizzard (C) swept down from the ridge, (D) burying half their supplies.
options: had the expedition set up camp
items.explanation: Hardly / scarcely … when is the fixed pair; than belongs only with no sooner.

items.q: (A) Demanding that the factory is closed immediately, (B) the residents (C) marched to the town hall (D) with a petition bearing a thousand signatures.
options: Demanding that the factory is closed immediately
with a petition bearing a thousand signatures
items.correction: Demanding that the factory be closed immediately
items.explanation: After demand that, the verb is in the subjunctive: be closed, not is closed.

items.q: The hikers, (A) who had set off before dawn, (B) collapsed beside the stream, (C) exhausting after the long climb, (D) and did not stir until sunset.
options: who had set off before dawn
and did not stir until sunset
items.explanation: The hikers feel the tiredness, so the past participle exhausted is needed; the -ing form describes what causes the feeling (an exhausting climb).

items.q: Anyone (A) wished to attend the astronomy lecture (B) must register online by Friday, (C) as seating in the observatory (D) is strictly limited.
options: wished to attend the astronomy lecture
items.correction: wishing to attend the astronomy lecture
items.explanation: A reduced relative clause with an active meaning (anyone who wishes) uses the present participle wishing; the past participle wished would give a passive meaning.

items.q: The guide told us (A) that the temple (B) had been built in the twelfth century and asked (C) whether had we visited (D) the older ruins nearby.
options: had been built in the twelfth century
items.explanation: A reported question keeps statement word order: asked whether we had visited, with no subject-auxiliary inversion.

items.q: The physicist, (A) whose theory was ridiculed at first, (B) has since received the prize (C) that every young researcher (D) dreams of winning it.
options: whose theory was ridiculed at first
items.explanation: The relative pronoun that already stands for the prize as the object of winning; repeating it with it creates a redundant pronoun.

items.q: (A) In spite of the fact that the river had burst its banks, (B) the farmers were reluctant (C) to abandon the livestock (D) which they were dependent of for their income.
options: In spite of the fact that the river had burst its banks
which they were dependent of for their income
items.correction: which they were dependent on for their income
items.explanation: The adjective dependent is followed by on (or upon), never of.

items.q: The twins (A) could not agree on (B) whom should carry the trophy (C) into the stadium, (D) so the coach decided for them.
options: so the coach decided for them
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of should carry, so it must be who; whom is only for objects, whatever preposition precedes the clause.

items.q: The Amazon, (A) whose basin remains (B) among the least mapped regions on Earth, (C) discharges (D) far more water than any river in the world.
options: among the least mapped regions on Earth
far more water than any river in the world
items.correction: far more water than any other river in the world
items.explanation: When something is compared with the group it belongs to, other is required: than any other river, otherwise the Amazon is being compared with itself.

items.q: By the time you read this, the committee (A) will already vote on the proposal (B) to extend the library's opening hours, (C) so please check the noticeboard (D) for the result.
options: will already vote on the proposal
to extend the library's opening hours
items.correction: will already have voted on the proposal
items.explanation: By the time + present simple marks a future deadline, so the action completed before it takes the future perfect: will already have voted.

items.q: Many philosophers have argued that (A) humanity's growing separation from (B) the nature (C) lies at the root (D) of our modern restlessness.
items.explanation: Nature meaning the natural world is an uncountable abstract noun used without the; the nature of means the character of something.

items.q: (A) Economics are in fact (B) one of the most useful subjects (C) a teenager can study, (D) however dry many pupils find it.
options: one of the most useful subjects
however dry many pupils find it
items.explanation: Names of academic subjects ending in -ics (economics, physics, mathematics) are singular: Economics is.

items.q: (A) Were the government to invest seriously in railways, (B) far fewer people (C) will rely on private cars (D) for their daily commute.
options: Were the government to invest seriously in railways
items.explanation: Were the government to… is an inverted second conditional (hypothetical), so the result clause needs would, not will.

items.q: (A) It was because of the dense fog (B) why the ferry (C) was held in the harbour (D) until well after noon.
options: It was because of the dense fog
items.explanation: A cleft sentence It was … that … uses that to introduce the rest, even when the emphasised element is a reason; why is not possible here.

items.q: The pilot, (A) whose licence has since been suspended, (B) admitted that he (C) had flown into the storm (D) and done a serious error of judgement.
options: whose licence has since been suspended
and done a serious error of judgement
items.correction: and made a serious error of judgement
items.explanation: Error and mistake collocate with make, not do: made a serious error of judgement.

items.q: Now that we have missed the train, (A) I wish we (B) had left earlier; if only (C) the guide told us (D) about the shortcut through the park.
options: about the shortcut through the park
items.explanation: If only about a past regret takes the past perfect, exactly like I wish we had left: if only the guide had told us.

items.q: The professor (A) patiently explained us (B) how the enzyme works, (C) using a model (D) built from coloured beads.
items.explanation: Explain does not take an indirect object directly: the pattern is explain something to someone, so explained to us how….

items.q: The parade (A) will be called off (B) and the floats returned to the warehouse (C) unless the rain (D) doesn't stop by noon.
options: and the floats returned to the warehouse
items.explanation: Unless already means if … not, so the verb after it must be positive: unless the rain stops.

items.q: At the border the officer (A) checked my passport twice, (B) asked me (C) how long I intended to stay (D) and where was I going next.
options: how long I intended to stay
and where was I going next
items.correction: and where I was going next
items.explanation: Reported questions keep statement order after the question word: where I was going, not where was I going.

items.q: (A) Seldom I have seen such a beautifully kept garden, (B) and rarely does its owner (C) allow visitors (D) to wander through it alone.
options: Seldom I have seen such a beautifully kept garden
items.correction: Seldom have I seen such a beautifully kept garden
items.explanation: A sentence opening with a negative adverb such as Seldom requires inversion: Seldom have I seen, just as in rarely does its owner allow.
